chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: Chicago versus New York musicians; first New York theaters

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: How do you see the difference between the Chicago musicians, you know, of the thirties, and New York musicians? The difference between the two -- two scenes?

It's very hard to say, because in the thirties, like when I was with Earl, like when we went to New York, I come to find out the majority of musicians, good musicians in New York were from Chicago. Was from the West.
That's right. That's right. But New York musicians I think still have a snobbish thing.

Yeah, you could always tell a New York musician, because like when we first went there, you had to go in and rehearse the show at the Apollo Theater, they had what they called -- the union had it, you had to have a stand-by band in the theater. Besides the stand-by band, all the New York musicians would make their rehearsal at night, like we opened up Friday morning, they'd make the rehearsal Thursday night. They'd be standing behind you, reading over your shoulder, see if you're playing it right. Able to step in right away in case you goof up. I never will forget that.
Yeah, the competition is a little
They had a little problem the first time we went there, when we throwed those strings on them, for the show.
And you played the Apollo then?
No, it was the Lafayette Theater.
Schiffman owned the Lafayette Theater, then the next time we went back it was the Harlem Opera House, owned by the same man, then the next time we went back it was the Apollo.
